entities.name: Macedonian dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Macedonian dynasty (867-1056 CE) was the ruling house of the Byzantine Empire during its greatest medieval flourishing, named for its founder Basil I's origins in Macedonia. The Macedonian period produced Byzantine civilization's highest achievements: the reconquest of Crete, Cyprus, and parts of Syria; the Christianization of Bulgaria, Serbia, and Kievan Rus; the creation of the Cyrillic alphabet by Cyril and Methodius (technically under their predecessors but supported by this dynasty); and a cultural renaissance that produced the finest Byzantine mosaics and manuscripts.

Basil I (r. 867-886 CE) founded the dynasty after murdering his way to power — first assassinating Emperor Michael III with whom he had an unusual intimate relationship, then ruling as one of Byzantium's most capable emperors. His successors Leo VI (the Wise), Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos (the Purple-Born), and Basil II (the Bulgar-Slayer) represent Byzantine civilization's literary, diplomatic, and military peaks respectively.

Basil II (r. 976-1025 CE), the dynasty's greatest military ruler, ended the Bulgarian First Empire by blinding 15,000 Bulgarian prisoners (leaving 1 eye per 100 to guide them home) — earning the name 'Bulgar-Slayer.' Yet Basil II's 49-year reign was also one of Byzantium's most stable, extending Byzantine territory to the Danube, expanding into Syria and Armenia, and converting Vladimir of Kiev to Christianity, spreading Orthodox Christianity to Russia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Macedonian dynasty's Christianization of the Slavs and the Cyrillic alphabet's creation represent Byzantium's most consequential cultural legacy — establishing the Orthodox Christian civilization that shaped Russia, Bulgaria, Serbia, and Eastern Europe.
